correctness.rationale: The uniform background gives f_X≥η/2 on (0,2); the square-map density of Y is f_X(√y)/(2√y) almost everywhere on (0,4) and is integrable even at zero by substitution. The two cdfs meet the strict interval-support condition, and Q_Y(F_X(x))=x² exactly. At levels (1/6,1/4,1/3), solving the discrete balance equations for J and J² gives coordinates (3/7,3/5,3/4) and (5/7,1,6/5), with successive slopes 5/3 and 4/3. If u_i and v_i are the continuous expectile coordinates, put D=(v₂−v₁)(u₃−u₂)−(v₃−v₂)(u₂−u₁). In the published Eq. (8), the left side minus right side is 2D/[(u₃−u₁)(v₃−v₁)], so D>0 violates it, as well as convexity. The expectile score is strongly decreasing in its threshold with constant min(α,1−α), and Lipschitz in the observation with constant max(α,1−α), hence the root shifts by at most five times the coupling L¹ distance at the three chosen levels. Here those distances are at most 3η and 12η, the latter using the 4-Lipschitz square map. Adjacent abscissa gaps remain positive; the pairwise ordinate and abscissa errors are at most 120η and 30η. The product error bound (372/7)η+7200η² leaves D≥74534937/8750000000>0 at the specified η. The constants and strict inequality were independently reproduced with exact arithmetic; replay: python3 /workspace/branches/3882fb2e-b9e5-407b-a2d5-8087ac90d2b0/record3_exact_check.py. The discrete calculation alone is not the continuous theorem. The implication is answered negatively; it was not a theorem asserted by Eberl–Klar.
residual_risks: The certificate concerns the discrete coordinates and perturbation constants; full-support absolute continuity and preservation of the strict sign require the accompanying analytic coupling proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The dispersive example's ordinary transformation slope drops from 5 to 1, so that pair does not satisfy the premise here. The smoothed s₂/sf pair also fails the ordinary convex-transform premise for small ε: at probabilities 0.14, 0.16 and 0.20 the X quantiles all lie in the first bump, while Y moves from the first to the second bump and then stays within the second. The first secant slope of Q_Y∘F_X then diverges as ε→0; the second is bounded since its numerator is at most 2ε² and its denominator is at least 0.04/sup f_X, of order at least ε². These are nearby order separations, not mechanical implications of the frozen one.
